items.title: Matrices don't commute — and that's why quantum mechanics works
items.claim: AB is not generally equal to BA for matrices. The order of operations matters. This isn't a defect — it's the most important feature of matrix algebra and the mathematical foundation of quantum uncertainty.

options.text: Matrices represent linear transformations of vectors; applying transformation A then B is generally not the same as B then A. The non-commutativity reflects that composition of transformations in higher dimensions does NOT commute in general
AB = BA always works for invertible matrices

items.reveal:
For matrices, AB and BA are generally different — and AB is well-defined only when A's columns equal B's rows. Even for square matrices of the same size, AB and BA can differ wildly.

Example: A = [[1, 1], [0, 1]], B = [[1, 0], [1, 1]].
AB = [[2, 1], [1, 1]].
BA = [[1, 1], [1, 2]]. Different.

When does AB = BA? Some special cases: scalar multiples of identity; same diagonal matrix; simultaneously diagonalisable matrices; powers of the same matrix.

The commutator [A, B] = AB - BA measures the non-commutativity. For ordinary numbers it's always zero; for matrices it can be anything.

In QUANTUM MECHANICS:
- Physical observables are represented as matrices (or operators on Hilbert space).
- The commutator of position and momentum: [x, p] = i * hbar. Non-zero!
- Heisenberg's uncertainty principle: the variance of two non-commuting observables, in any state, has a lower bound proportional to the commutator. You can't simultaneously know position and momentum precisely.

This is not a measurement limitation — it's a structural feature of the math. Eigenvectors of non-commuting matrices are different; states have to choose between definite x and definite p.

Lie groups and algebras: continuous symmetry transformations form groups whose generators are matrices with commutation relations. The group SU(3) underlies the strong nuclear force; SU(2) describes weak force and quantum spin; U(1) describes electromagnetism. The standard model of particle physics is built from non-commuting matrices.

In computer graphics: rotation matrices in 3D don't commute (mentioned in another card). The order matters when composing transformations.
items.why: Multiplication seems naturally commutative. For matrices it isn't — and the depth of this fact is that quantum mechanics, particle physics, computer graphics, and most of modern physics rely on it.

items.title: Completing the square was a geometric procedure 4000 years ago
items.claim: Babylonians (~1800 BC) solved quadratic equations using cut-and-paste geometric procedures. They literally cut a square into pieces and rearranged them. The algebraic 'completing the square' technique is the algebraic shadow of this physical manipulation.

options.text: It is a modern algebraic trick

x squared + bx can be VISUALISED as a square (x by x) plus a rectangle (b by x); cutting the rectangle in half and attaching each half to the square's adjacent sides produces an L-shape. Completing the missing corner adds (b/2) squared and gives a complete square of side (x + b/2)
It only works for special quadratics

items.reveal_title: Geometric origin of the quadratic formula
items.reveal:
Old Babylonian tablets (YBC 7289, c. 1800 BC) show problems like: 'I added the side of a square to its area and got 0.75. What is the side?'

The procedure: take half of 1 (the coefficient of the side) — that's 0.5. Square it — 0.25. Add to 0.75 — that's 1. Square root of 1 is 1. Subtract 0.5 — answer is 0.5.

What they were doing geometrically: visualise x^2 (a square) + x (a rectangle, 1 by x). Cut the rectangle in half (each piece is 1/2 by x). Attach one piece to each adjacent side of the square. You now have an L-shape with side (x + 1/2). Fill in the missing corner (1/2 by 1/2 = 1/4). Total area is x^2 + x + 1/4 = (x + 1/2)^2.

From x^2 + x = 0.75, add 1/4 to both sides: (x + 1/2)^2 = 1, so x + 1/2 = 1, x = 0.5.

The quadratic formula x = (-b plus/minus sqrt(b^2 - 4ac))/(2a) is this same procedure for ax^2 + bx + c = 0, fully generalised. Al-Khwarizmi (Baghdad, c. 825) gave the systematic algebraic version. The word 'algebra' comes from his treatise's title — 'al-jabr' meaning 'completion' or 'restoration', literally 'reassembling broken parts'.

Geometric algebra: an entire branch of mathematics treats algebraic identities as geometric statements. Many people find quadratics easier to remember when they can VISUALISE the completed square.
items.why: Quadratic formulas feel like magic algebra. They are the algebraic encoding of a physical cut-and-rearrange procedure that has been used for 4000 years.

items.title: The cubic formula forced mathematicians to take imaginary numbers seriously
items.claim: Cardano's 1545 formula for cubic equations works perfectly — but its intermediate steps require taking square roots of negative numbers, even when the final answer is a real number. The formula computes real answers via imaginary intermediates.
items.prompt: Why do imaginaries appear in real-answer cubics?

options.text: For cubics with three real roots, Cardano's formula expresses each root as a sum of two cube roots that individually are complex numbers; the imaginary parts cancel in the sum, but cannot be avoided algebraically — this is the 'casus irreducibilis'
Imaginary numbers can be avoided with smarter algebra
Cubics with real roots are computed without complex numbers

items.reveal_title: Casus irreducibilis and the unavoidability of complex numbers
items.reveal:
Cardano's formula for x^3 + px + q = 0:
x = cube root of (-q/2 + sqrt(q^2/4 + p^3/27)) + cube root of (-q/2 - sqrt(q^2/4 + p^3/27)).

When all three roots are real, q^2/4 + p^3/27 is NEGATIVE — so you must take square roots of negatives. The cube roots are complex; their sum is real.

Example: x^3 - 15x - 4 = 0 has solutions x = 4, x = -2 plus or minus sqrt(3). All real.

Cardano's formula gives:
x = cube root of (2 + 11i) + cube root of (2 - 11i)

It's verifiable that 2 + 11i = (2 + i)^3 and 2 - 11i = (2 - i)^3. So x = (2 + i) + (2 - i) = 4. Real answer, computed through imaginary intermediates.

This is called casus irreducibilis (Cardano's term). For three real roots, there is no trigonometric-free, complex-number-free formula. The need for complex numbers is essential, not an avoidable trick.

This forced 16th-17th century mathematicians to take the 'sophistic quantities' seriously. The cubic was the gateway that pushed complex numbers from curiosity into necessity. They would only become geometrically intuitive with Wessel/Argand/Gauss in the 1790s-1830s — but their usefulness was inescapable from 1545 onward.

The quartic was solved by Cardano's student Ferrari (also published in Ars Magna). The quintic, as Galois and Abel showed centuries later, cannot be solved by radicals at all.
items.why: Real-world problems suggest only real numbers. The algebra of cubics shows that even the simplest real-coefficient real-root polynomials force complex arithmetic in their solution. Imaginaries aren't optional.
